text: Welcome! At the very top of the slide you can see the problem child for today—the integral sign from zero to pi divided by eight of x times sine of two x.
Oh wow, so we’re juggling both an x and a sine all at once. Sounds like a tag-team match!
Exactly, and any time we see a product like this—polynomial times trigonometric—our favourite tool is Integration by Parts.
That’s the one with u and d v, right? The formula that says integral u d v equals u v minus integral v d u.
Perfect recall. Give yourself a gold star! We’ll also need two other friends: how to handle definite limits and how to integrate basic sine or cosine.
So prerequisite checklist: Integration by Parts, evaluating at limits, and knowing that the antiderivative of sine of two x is negative cosine of two x divided by two.
Bingo. Think of it like packing a hiking bag—we just made sure we have water, a map, and snacks before the trek.
Nice. And the trek ends at pi divided by eight.
Right. Before we dive in, quick question: which piece do you think we should designate as u when we use Integration by Parts?
Hmmm… my gut says pick u equals x because its derivative is super simple—just one.
Excellent intuition. We’ll test that formally in the next slide, but you’re already on the right trail.
Sweet! So the roadmap is: choose u and d v, apply the formula, integrate what’s left, then plug in zero and pi divided by eight.
Precisely. If we follow that roadmap, the numbers will line up beautifully—kind of like dominoes falling in slow motion.
I love domino math! Ready to push the first tile.
Let’s do it. Onward to choosing u and d v.
Look at the centre of the slide: u equals x in yellow, d v equals sine of two x d x in orange.
So I called it! Derivative of u gives us d u equals d x—nice and tidy.
Exactly. Now, we need v, the antiderivative of sine of two x.
Right—integrating sine of two x gives negative cosine of two x divided by two. I’ll jot v equals minus cosine of two x over two.
Great job. Notice how we picked d v to be the piece that integrates cleanly. That’s like choosing the smoothest gear for a bike climb.
And picking u equals x means the derivative d u is just one—like dropping extra luggage so the climb is easier.
Well said. Quick check: any sign errors we should watch out for when taking that antiderivative?
Yes, the minus sign that appears because the derivative of cosine is negative sine. So we’re good.
Perfect. One more tiny question: will any limits interfere with these choices?
Nope—the limits zero and pi divided by eight stay parked until the very end when we substitute into the antiderivative.
Exactly. Everything is staged. All set to plug into the Integration by Parts formula on the next slide?
Buckled in and ready!
Front and centre on the slide you can see the formula painted in yellow.
So plugging in, we get u v equals x times negative cosine of two x over two.
Nicely spoken. That’s the first term.
Then we subtract the integral of v d u, which is minus cosine of two x over two times d x.
Notice the double negative: one from v and one from the subtraction sign in the formula.
Ah, two negatives make a plus! So we actually add one-half times the integral of cosine of two x d x.
Exactly. The minus sign is sneaky—like a ninja hiding in plain sight. Catching it avoids disaster later.
So the expression is negative x cosine two x over two plus one-half integral cosine two x d x.
Spot on. The hard part is done; what remains is a simple cosine integral.
Which feels like dessert after the main course.
Delicious mathematical dessert indeed. Ready to take that last bite?
Bring on the whipped cream of integration!
Mid-slide you’ll see integral cosine of two x d x equals sine of two x divided by two.
That makes sense because the derivative of sine of two x is two cosine of two x.
Exactly. Multiplying by one-half cancels that extra two.
So we plug it in: we already had one-half out front, then another one-half from the antiderivative, giving one-quarter.
Great arithmetic. The full antiderivative is negative x cosine two x over two plus sine two x over four.
Let me sanity-check: if I differentiate that, I should recover x sine two x.
Go ahead—mentally differentiate.
First term: product rule gives negative cosine two x over two plus x times two sine two x over negative two—that simplifies to minus cosine two x over two plus x sine two x.
Add the derivative of sine two x over four, which is cosine two x divided by two.
The two cosine terms cancel! Yay, we’re left with x sine two x.
Exactly. Proof complete. You’ve earned a virtual fist bump.
*Fist bump!* Next stop: plugging in zero and pi divided by eight.
On the slide, you’ll see F of pi divided by eight worked out line by line.
First, substitute x equals pi divided by eight into negative x cosine two x over two.
Good. Two times pi divided by eight is pi divided by four.
Cosine of pi divided by four is square root of two over two, so that part becomes negative pi divided by eight times square root of two over two, all over two.
Nicely navigated. Now the sine term: sine of pi divided by four is also square root of two over two, divided by four gives square root of two over eight.
So F of pi divided by eight equals negative pi times square root of two over thirty-two plus square root of two over eight.
Perfect. Now evaluate F of zero.
Plugging in zero makes both sine and x vanish—so F of zero equals zero.
Therefore the definite integral is F of pi divided by eight minus F of zero, which is simply F of pi divided by eight.
Got it. All that’s left is a little algebra polish.
Exactly—let’s tidy the radicals and fractions next.
The slide shows the two terms with a common factor square root of two.
Yeah, I see negative pi square root of two over thirty-two and positive square root of two over eight.
Convert the second fraction to have denominator thirty-two: multiply numerator and denominator by four.
That gives four square root of two over thirty-two.
Perfect. Now factor out square root of two over thirty-two.
We’re left with square root of two over thirty-two times quantity four minus pi.
Exactly. A neat single fraction wearing a radical hat.
So the final answer is square root of two times open bracket four minus pi close bracket all over thirty-two.
Beautiful. Like condensing a winding mountain trail into one glorious panorama shot.
I’ll definitely remember this hike! Integration by Parts, careful sign work, and tidy algebra at the end.
Stellar work today. Keep that curiosity burning and those ninja minus signs in check!
Will do. Thanks for the guided adventure!
